correctness.rationale: The proof starts from the published exhaustive classification of near-perfect numbers with two prime factors into Types A, B, C and 40. For even base, \(U_n\) is odd. In Type A this forces \(U_n=(2^p-1)^2\), and Ljunggren excludes length above two because its only repunit-square bases give square roots 11 and 20, neither a Mersenne prime. Type B contradicts the digit bound. Type C forces \(U_n=q\), and length at least three contradicts \(U_n>2^{2t-2}\ge2^t>q\). The isolated value 40 is excluded directly. The converse follows by substitution into the standard Type-A and Type-C formulas. `verify.py` exactly checks the resulting families and exhausts a finite regression box.

value.rationale: The focal paper makes repdigit near-perfect numbers a stated research object and gives a finite small-base theorem. Removing the base bound on the entire natural subclass of even bases is a meaningful structural extension, and the result is stronger than a finiteness statement because it completely identifies the two surviving parametric families. The classification also explains why Type B and the exceptional value 40 can never occur in an even-base repdigit with at least two digits.
